title: Topical vancomycin powder and surgical site infection in cranial and spinal surgery: A prospective cohort study from Pakistan
content:
by Ihsan Ullah, Syed Shayan Shah, Muhammad Nawaz Khan, Sadia Shafique, Muhammad Junaid, Muhammad Sohaib Khan

Background

Surgical site infection is a major complication of neurosurgery, and its incidence is higher in low- and middle-income countries. Topical vancomycin powder has shown potential for preventing surgical site infection in high-income settings, but evidence from low- and middle-income countries is limited. This study assessed the association between the use of topical vancomycin powder and postoperative surgical site infection.

Methods

This prospective cohort study included 600 adult patients who underwent elective cranial or spinal neurosurgery at Lady Reading Hospital, Peshawar, Pakistan, between January 2021 and December 2024. Patients received topical vancomycin powder (1 g applied to the wound bed or subgaleal space before closure; n = 310) or standard care (n = 290). Surgical site infection was defined according to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention criteria. Multivariable logistic regression was performed to adjust for potential confounders, and adjustment for year of surgery and propensity score weighting were performed as sensitivity analyses.

Results

Baseline clinical characteristics were similar between groups, whereas the use of topical vancomycin increased over the study period. Surgical site infection occurred in 1.6% (5/310) of the vancomycin group and 6.6% (19/290) of controls (p = 0.003). The reduction was statistically significant in cranial procedures (1.6% vs 7.6%, p = 0.009) but not in spinal procedures (1.6% vs 5.0%, p = 0.165). Topical vancomycin was independently associated with a lower risk of surgical site infection (adjusted odds ratio 0.23, 95% confidence interval 0.08 to 0.63, p = 0.004), and the association persisted in all sensitivity analyses. No vancomycin-related adverse events or systemic toxicity were recorded.

Conclusion

Topical vancomycin powder was associated with a lower observed rate of surgical site infection after cranial and spinal neurosurgery in this single-center cohort from Pakistan, with no recorded toxicity. Because treatment allocation was not randomized, these findings do not establish efficacy, and randomized controlled trials are needed.
